phrases.translation: Ṭâ-Sĩn-Mĩm
phrases.explanation: The chapter opens with disconnected letters whose interpretation the commentary says has already been discussed. It connects them directly to the declaration that follows, that these are the verses of a clear Book sent down to Muhammad. The letters therefore stand at the threshold of revelation rather than as an isolated puzzle. Their mystery gives way to the claim that the Book itself makes its divine origin plain and was not invented by the Prophet.

phrases.translation: These are the verses of the clear Book
phrases.explanation: The Book is called clear because what it contains is manifest. The commentary says Allah's blessing, right guidance, and direction are perfectly clear in it. The word does not mean merely that the text is easy to read, but that it makes the truth evident. The phrase prepares for the story of Moses and Pharaoh, which will show divine guidance and judgment in the lives of earlier peoples.

phrases.translation: We narrate to you ˹O Prophet˺ part of the story of Moses and Pharaoh in truth for people who believe
phrases.explanation: Allah tells the Prophet that He recounts part of the story of Moses and Pharaoh in truth. The account is given for people who believe in the Book and accept it, so their hearts can be at ease. The commentary says the pattern matters for the Prophet's own opponents. Just as Allah destroyed Pharaoh and saved the Israelites, He can destroy those who oppose Muhammad and deliver the believers from them.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Pharaoh ˹arrogantly˺ elevated himself in the land and divided its people into ˹subservient˺ groups
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh exalted himself in Egypt through tyranny and injustice, subjugating the people until they acknowledged his enslavement. He divided them into separate groups, treating some differently from others. The commentary describes this division as a tool of rule, since he killed some, spared others, punished some, and enslaved others. His power is therefore shown as organized oppression rather than legitimate government.

phrases.translation: one of which he persecuted, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women. He was truly one of the corruptors
phrases.explanation: One group, identified in the commentary as the Israelites, was singled out for persecution. Their sons were slaughtered while their women were kept alive, and reports connect this policy to a dream or prediction that a boy from among them would bring about Egypt's ruin. Pharaoh is called a corrupter because he killed people without right, enslaved those he had no right to enslave, and was arrogant toward his Lord.

phrases.translation: But it was Our Will to favour those who were oppressed in the land
phrases.explanation: Allah's will is set against Pharaoh's oppression. He intends to favor the same people who had been weakened in the land, identified by the commentary as the Israelites. The phrase does not deny their present suffering but declares that it is not the final word. Divine favor is about to work through the very group Pharaoh treated as powerless, reversing the purpose of his cruelty.

phrases.translation: making them models ˹of faith˺ as well as successors
phrases.explanation: Allah intends to make the oppressed group models and successors. The commentary explains models as rulers or holders of authority, and successors as those who inherit the land after Pharaoh and his people are destroyed. The reversal is complete. Those who were enslaved will not only be delivered but will bear authority in the place of their former masters, because Allah's purpose outweighs Pharaoh's policy.

phrases.translation: and to establish them in the land
phrases.explanation: Allah will establish the delivered people firmly in the land. The commentary says this means preparing an abode for them in Syria and Egypt. Establishment is more than escape from danger. It is a settled place where the formerly oppressed can live with security and authority. The promise continues the reversal announced in the previous verse, moving from favor and inheritance to actual possession.

phrases.translation: and through them show Pharaoh, Hamân, and their soldiers ˹the fulfilment of˺ what they feared
phrases.explanation: Allah will also show Pharaoh, Haman, and their soldiers the very thing they feared. The commentary says they had been warned that ruin would come through a man from the Children of Israel, which is why Pharaoh killed their sons. Through Moses, Allah brings about their destruction and the ruin of their homes. Two accepted readings say either that Allah shows them this or that Pharaoh sees it, with the same outcome.

phrases.translation: We inspired the mother of Moses: “Nurse him, but when you fear for him, put him then into the river
phrases.explanation: Allah inspires Moses' mother to nurse him and, when she fears for him, to place him in the river. The commentary says this was a revelation cast into her heart, not prophethood, and identifies the river as the Nile. Reports differ about how long she waited before placing him there, but the essential command is clear. She is to care for him first, then entrust him to Allah when danger comes.

phrases.translation: and do not fear or grieve. We will certainly return him to you, and make him one of the messengers
phrases.explanation: The mother is told not to fear or grieve, because Allah will return the child to her and make him a messenger. The commentary says fear concerns Pharaoh or the river, while grief concerns separation from her child. The promise includes both a personal reunion for nursing and a public mission. The one she fears will kill him is the very tyrant to whom her son will eventually be sent.

phrases.translation: And ˹it so happened that˺ Pharaoh’s people picked him up, only to become their enemy and source of grief
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh's people find the child unexpectedly, as one picks up a lost object. The commentary preserves different reports about who found him, including the wife's servants, Pharaoh's daughter, or his helpers, without decisively choosing one. They take him expecting benefit, but the outcome is that he becomes their enemy in religion and a source of grief through the calamities Allah brings at his hand. Their intention and the result diverge.

phrases.translation: Surely Pharaoh, Hamân, and their soldiers were sinful
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh, Haman, and their soldiers are described as sinful against their Lord. The commentary says this is why Moses becomes an enemy and a cause of grief to them. The phrase gives the moral reason for the reversal in the first part of the verse. They are not victims of an arbitrary fate, since their own sin and hostility to Allah turn the child they rescued into the means of their ruin.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh’s wife said ˹to him˺, “˹This baby is˺ a source of joy for me and you. Do not kill him
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh's wife calls the child a source of joy for herself and her husband and asks that he not be killed. The commentary explains the phrase as an implied statement that the child is a comfort to them both. Reports add that Pharaoh accepted the description only for his wife, not for himself. Her intervention spares the child at a moment when Pharaoh intended to kill him, and her compassion becomes part of Allah's plan.

phrases.translation: Perhaps he may be useful to us or we may adopt him as a son.” They were unaware ˹of what was to come˺
phrases.explanation: The wife suggests that the child may benefit them or be adopted as a son. Reports differ about when she made this plea, but they agree that it prevented his death. The final clause says they were unaware of what was coming. The commentary prefers the meaning that Pharaoh's household did not realize their destruction would come through this child, though it records other explanations. Their practical kindness conceals a future they cannot see.

phrases.translation: And the heart of Moses’ mother ached so much that she almost gave away his identity
phrases.explanation: Moses' mother is overwhelmed by anguish until she nearly reveals that the child is hers. The commentary discusses whether her heart was empty of everything except thoughts of Moses or empty of the revelation and promise she had received. It prefers the first view, because her constant thought of him explains why she almost cried out that he was her son. The verse gives an honest picture of a mother's grief under divine command.

phrases.translation: had We not reassured her heart in order for her to have faith ˹in Allah’s promise˺
phrases.explanation: Allah strengthens her heart so she does not disclose the secret and remains among the believers. The commentary says He confirmed her in faith, guided her to keep silent, and made her certain of His promise. Her restraint is therefore not lack of feeling but a gift of steadiness from Allah. The same promise that told her to place the child in the river also enables her to wait for its fulfillment.

phrases.translation: And she said to his sister, “Keep track of him
phrases.explanation: The mother tells Moses' sister to follow his track and find out what happens to him. The commentary explains the command as tracing his footsteps or seeking news of him. Reports describe the sister looking for any word about whether the child is alive or has been lost in the river. The instruction is practical and loving, giving the family a way to remain connected to the child without exposing the mother.

phrases.translation: So she watched him from a distance, while they were unaware
phrases.explanation: The sister watches him from a distance, and Pharaoh's people do not realize she is his sister. The commentary says she does not approach him, so no one will connect her with the child. One report describes her watching from the riverbank as the chest moves along. Her quiet observation prepares the way for the next step, when the family's need for a nurse creates an opening for her to speak.

phrases.translation: And We had caused him to refuse all wet-nurses at first, so his sister suggested
phrases.explanation: Allah prevents Moses from accepting any wet-nurse before he is returned to his mother. The commentary says that every woman brought to him was refused, even though nursing him would have gained favor with Pharaoh. This refusal is not accidental but part of the plan to fulfill the promise made to his mother. Seeing the household's concern, his sister recognizes the opportunity to suggest a family who can care for him.

phrases.translation: Shall I direct you to a family who will bring him up for you and take good care of him
phrases.explanation: The sister asks whether she should direct them to a household that will care for the child sincerely. The commentary says the household is his own family, and that when they suspected she knew him, she explained that they would be well-disposed toward the king. Her words are careful enough to avoid disclosure while leading them to his mother. The question becomes the means by which Allah returns the child to the one who longs for him.

phrases.translation: This is how We returned him to his mother so that her heart would be put at ease, and not grieve
phrases.explanation: Allah returns Moses to his mother so her heart can be comforted and her grief over separation can end. The commentary says the return follows Pharaoh's household finding him, and it reverses the fear that he would be killed. Her earlier anguish had almost made her reveal the secret, but now the child is with her again. The promise that seemed to demand loss becomes the source of relief.

phrases.translation: and that she would know that Allah’s promise is ˹always˺ true. But most people do not know
phrases.explanation: The return also teaches her that Allah's promise is true. The commentary says He had promised both to restore the child and to make him a messenger, and He fulfilled what He said. Most people, especially the polytheists, do not know or believe that His promise is true. The verse therefore presents the family's reunion as a sign for the larger story that follows.

phrases.translation: And when he reached full strength and maturity, We gave him wisdom and knowledge
phrases.explanation: When Moses reaches full bodily strength and maturity, Allah gives him judgment and knowledge. The commentary says judgment means understanding of religion, reason, and pious deeds granted before prophethood, while reports differ about the age of maturity, mentioning thirty or forty years. The emphasis is not on a precise birthday but on complete preparation. Before he is sent as a messenger, he is formed in understanding and obedience.

phrases.translation: This is how We reward the good-doers
phrases.explanation: Allah says this is how He rewards those who do good. The commentary explains that Moses was rewarded for obedience and patience at Allah's command, and that the same pattern applies to messengers and servants who persevere, obey, and hold firmly to what Allah forbids. Wisdom and knowledge are therefore not random gifts. They are the fruit of a life already oriented toward obedience, and they prepare him for the trials that follow.

phrases.translation: ˹One day˺ he entered the city unnoticed by its people. There he found two men fighting
phrases.explanation: Moses enters the city when its people are heedless, identified in reports as Memphis at midday. The commentary records different reasons for his entry, including following Pharaoh, entering secretly out of fear, or returning after people had forgotten an earlier incident. It regards the safest statement as the one the verse itself gives. The moment is quiet and unguarded, but it brings him into a conflict that changes his life.

phrases.translation: one of his own people, and the other of his enemies. The man from his people called to him for help against his foe
phrases.explanation: Moses finds two men fighting, one from his own people and one from his enemies. The commentary identifies the first as an Israelite who shares Moses' religious faction and the second as a Copt from Pharaoh's people. The Israelite calls on Moses for help against the oppressor. The scene places Moses' loyalty and anger in a public setting, where defending one of his people quickly becomes more dangerous than he expects.

phrases.translation: So Moses punched him, causing his death. Moses cried, “This is from Satan’s handiwork. He is certainly a sworn, misleading enemy
phrases.explanation: Moses strikes the enemy with his fist and kills him, though the commentary says he did not intend the man's death. He immediately calls the act Satan's work, explaining that Satan inflamed his anger and misleads people by making ugly deeds appear attractive. The phrase is a confession of moral responsibility, not a denial of the blow. Moses recognizes that the anger behind his defense has led to an act he must repent.

phrases.translation: He pleaded, “My Lord! I have definitely wronged my soul, so forgive me
phrases.explanation: Moses turns to Allah and says he has wronged his soul. The commentary explains the wrong as killing a man whom he had not been commanded to kill, since a prophet should not take life without divine authorization. He asks Allah to conceal the transgression and not punish him for it. His prayer shows that he does not excuse the killing by appealing to good intentions or to the oppression he witnessed.

phrases.translation: So He forgave him, ˹for˺ He is indeed the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: Allah forgives Moses because He is All-Forgiving and Most Merciful. The commentary says He did not punish him for the transgression, and that He conceals the sins of those who return to Him in repentance. Mercy here is not indifference to the death of the man. It is the gracious response of Allah to a servant who recognizes his wrong, turns back, and asks for forgiveness rather than defending himself.

phrases.translation: Moses pledged, “My Lord! For all Your favours upon me
phrases.explanation: Moses begins by acknowledging Allah's favor. The commentary says the immediate favor is His forgiveness of the killing, and that Moses responds with a pledge. It also notes a variant reading in which he asks Allah not to make him a helper of criminals, turning the statement into a prayer rather than an oath. Both readings show the same concern. Gratitude for forgiveness leads him to seek distance from wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: I will never side with the wicked
phrases.explanation: Moses pledges never to support the wicked, meaning the polytheists and those who persist in wrongdoing. The commentary says he would never again assist a wrongdoer in wickedness, and it observes that people who make such strong declarations are often tested. The next incident becomes that test. His resolve is sincere, but he will have to learn how to act justly in a situation where anger and fear return.

phrases.translation: And so Moses became fearful, watching out in the city, when suddenly the one who sought his help the day before cried out to him again for help
phrases.explanation: After the killing, Moses spends the next morning in the city fearful and watchful. The commentary says he fears being seized and put to death, and waits to hear what people will say about the case. Then the same Israelite who had asked for help the day before calls out to him again, now fighting with another enemy. The repetition draws Moses back toward the kind of conflict that had already produced a death.

phrases.translation: Moses rebuked him, “Indeed, you are clearly a trouble-maker
phrases.explanation: Moses rebukes the man as clearly misguided, because he fought with one person yesterday and another today. The commentary says the rebuke is shaped by Moses' regret over the previous day's killing. Reports differ about whom he meant and about who felt threatened by his anger, but the phrase itself is a sharp judgment. It shows Moses trying to restrain a situation that his earlier intervention had made more volatile.

phrases.translation: Then when Moses was about to lay his hands on their foe, the enemy said, “O Moses
phrases.explanation: As Moses moves to strike the Copt who is an enemy to both men, the Israelite fears that Moses intends to strike him instead. The commentary says his earlier rebuke and visible anger make the man misunderstand the gesture. The cry of O Moses therefore comes from fear, not calm accusation. A private killing from the day before is about to become public because the man's alarm brings it into speech.

phrases.translation: Do you intend to kill me as you killed a man yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in the land. You do not intend to make peace
phrases.explanation: The Israelite asks whether Moses intends to kill him as he killed a man the day before, and accuses him of wanting to be a tyrant rather than a peacemaker. The commentary explains tyranny as killing without right or retaliation, while peacemaking means acting in obedience to Allah for the benefit of people. The accusation is unfair in its fear, but it reveals the secret. The Copt hears it and carries the news to Pharaoh's authorities.

phrases.translation: And there came a man, rushing from the farthest end of the city. He said, “O Moses
phrases.explanation: A man comes hurrying from the farthest part of the city after the previous day's killing becomes known. The commentary says the Israelite's words were overheard and reported, prompting Pharaoh to order Moses' death. Reports differ about the messenger's name and sometimes identify him as a believer from Pharaoh's family. What matters is that he reaches Moses before the executioners, turning secret counsel into a warning.

phrases.translation: The chiefs are actually conspiring against you to put you to death, so leave ˹the city˺. I really advise you ˹to do so˺
phrases.explanation: The messenger tells Moses that the chiefs are deliberating to kill him and advises him to leave. The commentary says the warning is sincere counsel, not rumor. The conspiracy is now official, so Moses can no longer remain safely in the city. The verse shows Allah's deliverance arriving through a human act of loyalty and courage, as one person riskily carries news that gives the future prophet time to escape.

phrases.translation: So Moses left the city in a state of fear and caution, praying, “My Lord
phrases.explanation: Moses leaves the city in fear, watching for pursuit. The commentary says he fears being seized for the killing and keeps looking back lest the pursuers overtake him. One report says he did not yet know which direction to take. His departure is therefore both urgent and uncertain. He has left Pharaoh's household and power behind, but safety is not yet visible to him.

phrases.translation: Deliver me from the wrongdoing people
phrases.explanation: Moses prays, My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people. The commentary explains the wrongdoing people as the unbelievers who wronged themselves through their disbelief. The prayer is brief because the danger is immediate. He does not claim strength or a plan of his own, but asks Allah for rescue from a community whose authority is now turned against him.

phrases.translation: And as he made his way towards Midian, he said
phrases.explanation: Turning toward Midian means leaving Egypt and Pharaoh's authority behind. The commentary says Midian was associated with the people of Shu'ayb and that Moses set out without provisions, mount, or clear knowledge of the route. Reports describe hunger, bare feet, and an angel who showed him the way. The phrase marks a transition from royal life to hardship, and from danger to trust.

phrases.translation: I trust my Lord will guide me to the right way
phrases.explanation: Moses says he hopes his Lord will guide him to the right way. The commentary explains the right way as the road to Midian or the straight path, and says he spoke because he did not know the route. The word perhaps expresses trust rather than doubt in Allah. He has no map and little provision, but he relies on the Lord who can make the unknown road known.

phrases.translation: When he arrived at the well of Midian, he found a group of people watering ˹their herds˺
phrases.explanation: At the water of Midian Moses finds a large group of people watering their livestock. The commentary describes them as a multitude with cattle and sheep. The scene is ordinary pastoral work, but it also establishes a social order in which the strong have first access to the water. Moses arrives as a stranger with no status, yet his strength will soon change the situation for two vulnerable women.

phrases.translation: Apart from them, he noticed two women holding back ˹their herd˺. He asked ˹them˺, “What is the problem
phrases.explanation: Moses also notices two women holding back their flock and asks about their condition. The commentary discusses whether they held the sheep back from the water or kept people away from the sheep, preferring the first. Moses asks out of concern for their weakness and separation from the crowd. His question is not idle curiosity but the beginning of an act of help.

phrases.translation: They replied, “We cannot water ˹our animals˺ until the ˹other˺ shepherds are done, for our father is a very old man
phrases.explanation: The women explain that they cannot water until the shepherds have finished, and that their father is very old. The commentary says they wait for what remains in the troughs because they cannot push in among the men, while their father is too weak to do the work. Their explanation reveals both need and dignity. They are not asking for charity, but Moses recognizes an injustice in their delay.

phrases.translation: So he watered ˹their herd˺ for them, then withdrew to the shade and prayed, “My Lord
phrases.explanation: Moses waters the women's flock for them. Reports say he removed a heavy stone from the well or drew a large amount of water, enabling their sheep to drink before the other herders had finished. He then turns to the shade, identified as an acacia tree. The movement from decisive help to quiet withdrawal shows that he does not linger to demand a reward for what he has done.

phrases.translation: I am truly in ˹desperate˺ need of whatever provision You may have in store for me
phrases.explanation: In the shade Moses prays that he needs whatever good Allah may send down. The commentary says he was severely hungry and that the good he sought was food, with some reports adding that he let the women hear the prayer. His words are both a confession of dependence and a discreet request. After helping others, he places his own need before Allah without imposing on them.

phrases.translation: Then one of the two women came to him, walking bashfully
phrases.explanation: One of the two women returns to Moses, walking with bashfulness. The commentary says she covered her face with her garment or hand and was not brazen in her movement. Reports add that Moses asked her to walk behind him and describe the way, so that he would not look at her. Her modesty and his restraint are both emphasized, showing that the invitation which follows is conducted with dignity.

phrases.translation: She said, “My father is inviting you so he may reward you for watering ˹our animals˺ for us
phrases.explanation: The woman tells Moses that her father invites him in order to reward him for watering their animals. Reports say the father was surprised by how quickly the flock returned satisfied, asked his daughters what had happened, and then sent one of them back. The invitation is therefore an acknowledgment of a real service. Moses' earlier act of help becomes the occasion for hospitality and for a new stage in his life.

phrases.translation: When Moses came to him and told him his whole story, the old man said, “Have no fear! You are ˹now˺ safe from the wrongdoing people
phrases.explanation: When Moses meets the father and tells him his whole story, the old man reassures him that he has escaped the wrongdoing people. The commentary explains that Pharaoh and his people have no authority in this land. The phrase answers Moses' earlier prayer for deliverance. What began as flight from danger now becomes safety, hospitality, and the promise of a settled relationship with a household outside Pharaoh's reach.

phrases.translation: One of the two daughters suggested, “O my dear father! Hire him
phrases.explanation: One of the daughters advises her father to hire Moses. The commentary says she means employing him to tend the livestock, and it records several names and identities for the father, including a relative of Shu'ayb or Shu'ayb himself, without settling the dispute. The narrative needs only the old man's role as head of the household. The daughter's advice turns a stranger's single act of help into an ongoing place within the family.

phrases.translation: The best man for employment is definitely the strong and trustworthy ˹one˺
phrases.explanation: The daughter says the best person to hire is strong and trustworthy. The commentary explains strength as the ability to guard and care for the livestock, shown when Moses watered the flock and moved the heavy stone. Trustworthiness is shown by his lowered gaze and his care not to exploit her vulnerability on the way to her father. Her judgment is practical and moral, joining physical ability with integrity.

phrases.translation: The old man proposed, “I wish to marry one of these two daughters of mine to you
phrases.explanation: The father offers Moses one of his two daughters in marriage. The commentary discusses the names of the women and which one was intended, with reports identifying the one who had invited him. It also notes disagreement about the father's identity. The offer is not a reward forced on Moses but a proposal that joins marriage to a period of service, giving the stranger both family and obligation in Midian.

phrases.translation: provided that you stay in my service for eight years. If you complete ten, it will be ˹a favour˺ from you
phrases.explanation: The condition is that Moses serve the father for eight years, with ten years as a voluntary extra. The commentary explains the service as pasturing livestock and treats it as the bridal gift for the marriage. The longer term is not demanded. This detail shows care in defining the obligation, so the agreement does not become an open-ended claim on Moses' labor.

phrases.translation: but I do not wish to make it difficult for you. Allah willing, you will find me an agreeable man
phrases.explanation: The father says he does not wish to make the matter difficult and promises, Allah willing, to be among the righteous. The commentary explains this as good companionship and faithful fulfillment of what he has said. The proposal is therefore framed by fairness rather than exploitation. The father offers marriage, sets a clear term, and commits himself to honor the agreement he asks Moses to accept.

phrases.translation: Moses responded, “˹Then˺ it is ˹settled˺ between you and I
phrases.explanation: Moses accepts, saying the matter is settled between them. The commentary explains that the agreement about marriage and service is binding on both sides. His answer is brief and clear, with no attempt to renegotiate the terms. The verse presents a lawful covenant made in ordinary life, where trust, work, and family are joined under Allah's witness rather than left to vague custom.

phrases.translation: Whichever term I fulfill, there will be no ˹further˺ obligation on me. And Allah is a Witness to what we say
phrases.explanation: Moses says that whichever of the two terms he fulfills, there should be no further claim against him, and Allah is witness to their words. The commentary explains the terms as eight or ten years, and says Allah guards and witnesses what each party owes. Reports add that Moses completed the longer term. The phrase protects him from being held to more than the agreed service.

phrases.translation: When Moses had completed the term and was travelling with his family, he spotted a fire on the side of Mount Ṭûr
phrases.explanation: Moses completes the agreed term and travels with his family. Reports say he fulfilled the longer and more complete term of ten years, with some adding another ten years of service. The commentary says he is traveling toward Egypt when he perceives a fire by the Mount. The long period of ordinary work in Midian ends at this moment. A journey taken for family reasons becomes the beginning of prophethood.

phrases.translation: He said to his family, “Stay here, ˹for˺ I have spotted a fire
phrases.explanation: Moses tells his family to remain where they are because he has perceived a fire. The commentary explains the verb as seeing or perceiving, and the fire is on the side of Mount Tur. He does not yet know what the fire is, only that it may offer help. His instruction is practical and protective, leaving his family in safety while he goes to investigate what might be an ordinary source of light.

phrases.translation: Perhaps from there I can bring you some directions or a torch from the fire so you may warm yourselves
phrases.explanation: Moses hopes to bring back either news or a burning brand so his family can warm themselves. The commentary explains the brand as a piece of wood or root carrying fire, and says the need was warmth from winter cold. Accepted recitations differ in the word's vowels but not its meaning. The search begins with bodily need, yet it leads to the divine call that will change his mission.

phrases.translation: But when he came to it, he was called from the bush in the sacred ground to the right side of the valley
phrases.explanation: When Moses reaches the fire, the call comes from the right side of the valley, in a blessed plain, from a tree. The commentary explains the right side as the valley's bank on Moses' right, and records different reports about the kind of tree without settling the identification. The place is marked as sacred because Allah addresses him there. The fire is not itself the object of worship but the setting of revelation.

phrases.translation: O Moses! It is truly I. I am Allah—the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The call identifies the speaker as Allah, the Lord of all worlds. The wording stresses that it is truly He who addresses Moses, so the voice is not an angel speaking on His own authority. The title Lord of all worlds connects the private encounter in the valley with universal sovereignty. The One who owns every realm now commissions Moses to confront Pharaoh, the ruler who claimed lordship for himself.

phrases.translation: Now, throw down your staff!” But when he saw it slithering like a snake, he ran away without looking back
phrases.explanation: Allah commands Moses to throw down his staff, and it becomes a moving serpent. The commentary describes the creature as a large kind of snake, and says Moses turns away in flight without looking back or waiting. The sign is real enough to frighten him. His reaction recalls the earlier staff of his shepherding life, now transformed into a proof that ordinary objects obey their Creator.

phrases.translation: ˹Allah reassured him,˺ “O Moses! Draw near, and have no fear. You are perfectly secure
phrases.explanation: Allah tells Moses to draw near and not fear, because he is among the secure. The commentary says he is safe from harm by the serpent, which is only his staff under Allah's power. The reassurance does not remove the sign but gives Moses confidence in the One who produced it. Fear is answered by a command to approach, preparing him to receive the second proof and the mission that follows.

phrases.translation: Now put your hand through ˹the opening of˺ your collar, it will come out ˹shining˺ white, unblemished
phrases.explanation: Moses is told to put his hand into the opening of his garment, and it comes out shining white without disease. The commentary explains that the whiteness is not leprosy or a skin ailment, and one report says the hand shone like a lamp. The transformation is a sign, not an illness. It gives Moses a second visible proof from Allah, alongside the staff, that his message has divine authority.

phrases.translation: And cross your arms tightly to calm your fears
phrases.explanation: Moses is told to press his arm or forearm to himself because of fear. The commentary connects the gesture with the fright caused by seeing the serpent and notes two accepted recitations of the word for fear. The action is both physical and calming, drawing his arm close after the alarming sign. Allah's instruction acknowledges human terror rather than rebuking it, giving Moses a way to steady himself before his mission.

phrases.translation: These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs. They have truly been a rebellious people
phrases.explanation: The staff and the shining hand are two proofs from Allah for Pharaoh and his chiefs. The commentary calls them signs and arguments that confirm Moses' prophethood. They are sent to a people described as rebellious or unbelieving, who will need clear evidence because their hearts are set against the truth. The verse gathers the previous commands into a purpose, since the miracles are not displays but a message to confront tyranny.

phrases.translation: Moses appealed, “My Lord
phrases.explanation: Moses responds to the divine commission with an appeal to his Lord. The short address shows that he takes his fear directly to Allah rather than hiding it or refusing the task outright. It also prepares for the concrete objection that follows. The encounter in the sacred valley has given him signs, but he still has to face a dangerous past when he returns to Egypt.

phrases.translation: I have indeed killed a man from them, so I fear they may kill me
phrases.explanation: Moses says he killed one of Pharaoh's people and fears they will kill him. The commentary adds that he worries about being unable to defend himself clearly because of an impediment in his tongue. His fear is therefore both legal and personal, since he returns as someone wanted for a death. The objection is honest, and Allah's response will address it by giving him support rather than dismissing the danger.

phrases.translation: And my brother Aaron is more eloquent than I
phrases.explanation: Moses says his brother Aaron is more eloquent than he is. The commentary explains this as Aaron's greater ability to express what he intends, especially in a setting where Moses feels his own speech is inadequate. The request is not a complaint about Allah's choice but a plea for help. Moses recognizes the demands of the mission and asks for the human support that will make the message clear.

phrases.translation: so send him with me as a helper to support what I say, for I truly fear they may reject me
phrases.explanation: Moses asks Allah to send Aaron with him as a helper who will support and clarify his words, because he fears rejection. The commentary says two witnesses are more readily believed than one, and that Aaron can explain what Moses addresses to the people. It also notes accepted recitations of the verb. The request joins eloquence with credibility, addressing both Moses' speech difficulty and the audience's likely denial.

phrases.translation: Allah responded, “We will assist you with your brother and grant you both authority, so they cannot harm you
phrases.explanation: Allah promises to strengthen Moses through his brother and give them both authority, so Pharaoh's people cannot harm them. The commentary explains authority as a proof, and the image of strengthening the arm as support and protection. The response answers Moses' fear of being killed. His brother is granted as a helper, and the signs become the protective authority that makes their message effective.

phrases.translation: With Our signs, you and those who follow you will ˹certainly˺ prevail
phrases.explanation: Allah says that Moses, Aaron, and those who follow them will prevail through His signs. The commentary explains victory as overcoming Pharaoh and his courtiers by Allah's proof and power. The promise extends beyond the two brothers to the believers who join them. The outcome is not based on political strength but on the signs Allah gives, which turn a vulnerable group into the victorious party.

phrases.translation: But when Moses came to them with Our clear signs, they said ˹arrogantly˺, “This is nothing but conjured magic ˹tricks˺
phrases.explanation: Moses comes to Pharaoh and his court with clear signs, but they call them fabricated magic. The commentary says the signs are evidences that testify to the truth of his message, while the accusation dismisses them as sorcery invented by Moses. Their rejection is therefore not due to lack of clarity. They relabel a divine proof as a human trick in order to avoid its claim.

phrases.translation: We have never heard of this in ˹the history of˺ our forefathers
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh's people add that they never heard of such a thing among their forefathers. The commentary explains the thing they reject as the worship of the one God to whom Moses calls them. Their appeal to ancestral custom becomes an argument against truth, even though the signs are present. The verse shows how inherited practice can be used to resist a message that calls for a change in worship.

phrases.translation: Moses responded, “My Lord knows best who has come with ˹true˺ guidance from Him and will fare best in the end
phrases.explanation: Moses answers that his Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him and who will have the best final outcome. The commentary praises the courtesy of this reply, since Moses does not directly insult Pharaoh even though he could have. He leaves judgment to Allah while still making the issue clear. The question is not who appears powerful now but who stands on truth and will fare well at the end.

phrases.translation: Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed
phrases.explanation: Moses concludes that wrongdoers will never succeed. The commentary explains this as disbelievers not attaining their goal, and says the statement refers especially to Pharaoh. It is a restrained but firm judgment after the courteous appeal to Allah's knowledge. The verse closes the exchange by shifting attention from present power to final failure, since the one who rejects guidance cannot ultimately prosper.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh declared, “O chiefs! I know of no other god for you but myself. So bake bricks out of clay for me
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh tells his chiefs that he knows no god for them besides himself. The commentary explains this as a denial that they should worship the Lord to whom Moses calls them. He orders Haman to bake bricks from clay, and reports say he was the first to build with baked brick. His claim to divinity is joined to a construction project, as though human architecture could challenge the heavenly Lord.

phrases.translation: O Hamân, and build a high tower so I may look at the God of Moses, although I am sure he is a liar
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh wants a lofty tower so he can look upon the God of Moses, while accusing Moses of lying. The commentary says he wanted to see the object of Moses' worship and rejects the claim that such a Lord sent him. Reports describe the tower and even an arrow shot toward heaven, but the point is his arrogance. He tries to turn the unseen God into something he can inspect and conquer.

phrases.translation: And so he and his soldiers behaved arrogantly in the land with no right
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh and his soldiers behave arrogantly in Egypt without any right. The commentary says their pride is shown in refusing to believe Moses, reject Allah's oneness, and acknowledge their servitude to Him. Their political power becomes rebellion against their Lord. The phrase with no right makes clear that their claim to greatness has no moral or divine basis, even if it dominates the land for a time.

phrases.translation: thinking they would never be returned to Us
phrases.explanation: They assume they will never be returned to Allah. The commentary explains this as disbelief in resurrection, reward, and punishment, so they follow their desires without expecting accountability. Their mistake is not only intellectual but practical, since they act as though no one sees or will repay their deeds. The verse therefore connects denial of the Hereafter with tyranny, because those who expect no return lose a restraint on their conduct.

phrases.translation: So We seized him and his soldiers, casting them into the sea
phrases.explanation: Allah seizes Pharaoh and his soldiers and casts them into the sea. The commentary says He gathered them and drowned them, with one report naming a sea behind Egypt. The verb suggests being thrown away like something worthless. The same people who claimed divine status and built a tower to challenge heaven are overwhelmed by water, a creation entirely outside their control.

phrases.translation: See then what was the end of the wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to consider the end of the wrongdoers. The commentary says he should look with the eye of the heart at how Allah destroyed Pharaoh's people and gave their dwellings and possessions to the oppressed believers. The command also warns the Quraysh that rejection can bring the same outcome. The story of Moses is therefore not distant history but a pattern for the Prophet's own opponents.

phrases.translation: We made them leaders inviting ˹others˺ to the Fire
phrases.explanation: Allah makes Pharaoh and his people leaders who invite others to the Fire. The commentary explains that they become examples followed by those who are arrogant against Allah and reject Him, calling people to the deeds that lead to punishment. Their influence does not end with their own sin. In leading others astray, they multiply their wrongdoing and become responsible for a wider corruption.

phrases.translation: And on the Day of Judgment they will not be helped
phrases.explanation: On the Day of Resurrection they will have no helpers. The commentary says that when Allah punishes them, no one will stand by them, and the mutual support they enjoyed in worldly life will vanish. The phrase reverses their former power, since kings and soldiers depend on allies. In the final judgment, every human alliance proves useless before the One they defied.

phrases.translation: We caused a curse to follow them in this world
phrases.explanation: A curse follows Pharaoh's people in this world. The commentary explains this as disgrace, wrath, ruin, destruction, and an evil remembrance from Allah. Their punishment is not only physical drowning but also the loss of honor in history. The story itself becomes part of the curse, since later generations remember them as an example of arrogance and rejection rather than greatness.

phrases.translation: And on the Day of Judgment they will be among the outcasts
phrases.explanation: On the Day of Resurrection they will be among the outcasts. The commentary says another curse will overwhelm them with lasting disgrace and inseparable humiliation. It also says Allah makes them an instructive lesson and admonition for those willing to learn. The phrase therefore joins this world and the next, so their ruin is both an event in history and a continuing warning about unbelief.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We gave Moses the Scripture—after destroying earlier nations—as an insight for the people
phrases.explanation: Allah gave Moses the Scripture after destroying earlier nations. The commentary identifies these as communities such as the people of Noah, Ad, Thamud, Lot, and Midian. The Torah is called an insight for the people, meaning a light for the Children of Israel in religious matters. It comes after a long history of judgment, so revelation is presented as guidance given to a surviving generation.

phrases.translation: a guide, and mercy so perhaps they would be mindful
phrases.explanation: The Scripture is also a guide and mercy so people may remember. The commentary explains guidance as clarification and mercy as something received by those who act according to it. The purpose is that they remember Allah's favors, thank Him, and avoid ingratitude. The verse therefore describes revelation as both instruction and kindness, meant to shape memory and conduct rather than merely preserve laws.

phrases.translation: You were not there ˹O Prophet˺ on the western side of the mountain when We entrusted the Commandments to Moses
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is reminded that he was not on the western side of the mountain when Allah gave Moses His command. The commentary explains this as the time when Allah decreed obligations for Moses and his people and took him into a covenant. Muhammad did not witness that event. The verse emphasizes the distance between the Prophet's lifetime and the earlier revelation he recounts.

phrases.translation: nor were you present ˹in his time˺
phrases.explanation: The Prophet was not among the eyewitnesses of Moses' time. The commentary repeats that he was not present, so the story he tells cannot be explained as personal observation or ordinary historical memory. This prepares the claim that his knowledge comes by revelation. The detail strengthens the proof of prophethood, since he accurately recounts events he could not have seen.

phrases.translation: But We ˹later˺ raised ˹several˺ generations, and the ages took their toll on them
phrases.explanation: Allah raised many generations after Moses, and long ages passed over them. The commentary says communities were brought into being and their lifespans stretched out, so the events became distant from the Prophet's own time. The phrase explains why a fresh messenger is needed. Human memory and inherited tradition had been stretched over centuries, making direct knowledge of those events impossible.

phrases.translation: Nor were you living among the people of Midian, rehearsing Our revelations with them
phrases.explanation: The Prophet did not live among the people of Midian, reciting Allah's revelations to them. The commentary explains that he was not a sojourner there with the Scripture. His knowledge of Moses' stay in Midian is therefore not derived from contact with that community. The verse continues to remove ordinary sources of information, pointing instead to divine sending as the origin of the narrative.

phrases.translation: But it is We Who have sent ˹this revelation to you˺
phrases.explanation: Allah is the One who sent the revelation. The commentary says the Prophet witnessed none of these earlier events, but Allah did them and sent messengers, and now He has sent Muhammad with knowledge of them. The phrase shifts from negation to affirmation. The absence of eyewitness experience does not weaken the message, because its true source is the One who knows all history.

phrases.translation: And you were not at the side of Mount Ṭûr when We called out ˹to Moses˺
phrases.explanation: The Prophet was not at the side of Mount Tur when Allah called Moses. The commentary connects the call with the earlier covenant and includes reports that Allah addressed the future community of Muhammad with favor before they asked. Whether understood as the Mosaic call or a wider divine address, the point is the same. The Prophet's knowledge of the scene comes from Allah, not from attendance.

phrases.translation: But ˹you have been sent˺ as a mercy from your Lord to warn a people to whom no warner has come before you, so perhaps they may be mindful
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is sent as a mercy from his Lord to warn a people who had received no warner before him. The commentary identifies them as the Arabs living in idolatry and explains prophethood or the Quran itself as the mercy. The warning aims to bring them to mindfulness, so they recognize the error of unbelief and return to Allah's oneness. Mercy and warning are therefore not opposites.

phrases.translation: Also so they would not say, if struck by an affliction for what their hands have done: “Our Lord
phrases.explanation: Allah explains that He sent the Prophet so people could not claim an excuse when punishment came for their deeds. The commentary says affliction means chastisement and retribution for disbelief, sins, and transgressions. Without a prior messenger, they could argue that no warning had reached them. Sending the Prophet removes that argument, since guidance now comes before judgment.

phrases.translation: If only You had sent us a messenger, we would have followed Your revelations and become believers
phrases.explanation: They would say that if only Allah had sent a messenger, they would have followed His signs and become believers. The commentary explains this as following the proofs and Book revealed to the messenger and affirming His commands and prohibitions. The excuse sounds pious, but the surrounding verses show that many still reject the truth when it comes. The messenger is sent so that humanity has no claim against Allah after warning.

phrases.translation: But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, “If only he was given the like of what Moses had been given
phrases.explanation: When the truth comes from Allah, the deniers ask why Muhammad was not given something like what Moses received. The commentary says some reports connect this demand to Jews instructing the Quraysh to ask for a Book like the Torah. The request appears to honor Moses but functions as a rejection of the messenger before them. It sets one revelation against another instead of accepting either.

phrases.translation: Did they not deny what had been given to Moses earlier
phrases.explanation: The question reminds them that people had already denied what Moses was given. The commentary says this refers especially to the Jews who knew the earlier scripture but rejected it, and it exposes the inconsistency of the demand. If the gift given to Moses was not accepted when it came, asking for its like is not a sincere search for guidance. The objection is a pretext for unbelief.

phrases.translation: They claimed, “Both ˹Scriptures˺ are works of magic, supporting each other!” Adding, “We truly deny both
phrases.explanation: They call the two revelations works of magic that support each other and declare that they reject both. The commentary records different accepted readings and interpretations, including two sorcerers or two scriptures, and prefers a reading that refers to the books. It also notes disagreement about which books are meant. The central charge is clear. They dismiss connected revelations as collusion and refuse them together.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Bring then a scripture from Allah which is a better guide than these two so I may follow it, if your claim is true
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to challenge those who dismiss the earlier scriptures as magic. If they are truthful, let them bring a Book from Allah that guides better than the two they reject. The commentary says the challenge concerns the Torah and the Gospel, or the Torah and the Quran in other interpretations. The demand exposes their claim. If they cannot produce better guidance, their objection is shown to be empty.

phrases.translation: So if they fail to respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires
phrases.explanation: If they cannot answer the challenge, the Prophet is to know that they follow only their desires. The commentary says their accusation against the Books is a lie, and that they abandon the truth even while recognizing it. The statement is addressed to the Prophet but is meant to expose his opponents. Their rejection is not a search for better evidence but a refusal to submit what they want to Allah's guidance.

phrases.translation: And who could be more astray than those who follow their desires with no guidance from Allah
phrases.explanation: No one is further from the right path than a person who follows desire without guidance from Allah. The commentary explains guidance as clarification and covenant from Allah, which such people abandon in favor of the devil's obedience. Desire becomes a ruler when revelation is rejected. The rhetorical question therefore warns that the problem is not lack of information alone but a will that has chosen its own preference over divine instruction.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people
phrases.explanation: Allah does not guide wrongdoing people. The commentary says this refers to those who transgress His command, abandon obedience, deny His messenger, alter His covenant, and follow their desires. He does not lead them to the path by which they might attain truth. The statement is not arbitrary exclusion but the consequence of persistent rebellion. Those who refuse guidance place themselves outside the direction they claim to seek.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We have steadily delivered the Word ˹of Allah˺ to the people so they may be mindful
phrases.explanation: Allah has conveyed His Word to people in a connected sequence so they may take heed. The commentary explains this as successive reports about earlier communities, what happened to them when they denied messengers, and what will happen to those who imitate them. Interpretations differ about whether the address concerns Quraysh, Jews, or a specific group of believers, but the purpose is the same. Repeated warnings are given so people remember.

phrases.translation: ˹As for˺ those ˹faithful˺ to whom We had given the Scripture before this ˹Quran˺, they do believe in it
phrases.explanation: Those who received Scripture before the Quran and remained faithful believe in this new revelation. The commentary identifies them as People of the Book who recognized Muhammad and held him to be true, and reports mention a small group who came to him and suffered for their faith. Their belief contrasts with the denial of those who had no Book. Prior knowledge, when joined to sincerity, becomes a bridge to faith rather than a barrier.

phrases.translation: When it is recited to them, they declare, “We believe in it
phrases.explanation: When the Quran is recited to these believers, they say they believe in it. The commentary says they accept it as true and do not treat the new recitation as a rival to the earlier Books they already revered. Their response is immediate and public. Instead of demanding signs or arguing over the messenger's authority, they recognize the truth of what is recited and align themselves with it.

phrases.translation: This is definitely the truth from our Lord. We had already submitted ˹even˺ before this
phrases.explanation: They declare that the Quran is the truth from their Lord and that they were already submitted before it came. The commentary explains that they believed in earlier prophets and scriptures, and that their Books contained the description of Muhammad, so they had faith before the Quran's descent. Their submission is therefore continuous. The new revelation confirms the faith they already held rather than creating a separate religion.

phrases.translation: These ˹believers˺ will be given a double reward for their perseverance
phrases.explanation: These believers will receive a double reward because of their perseverance. The commentary records several explanations of that patience, including steadfastness on the first Book and then on following Muhammad, faith in him before his sending and obedience when he came, or endurance of harm after conversion. The common point is fidelity across two moments of guidance. Their reward matches a faith that remained firm through change and trial.

phrases.translation: responding to evil with good, and for donating from what We have provided for them
phrases.explanation: They also respond to evil with good and spend from what Allah has provided. The commentary says good deeds ward off evil ones, and that their spending occurs in obedience to Allah, including charity to the needy and maintaining family ties. Their faith is not private conviction. It produces moral resistance to wrong and generous use of wealth, so perseverance is joined to active goodness.

phrases.translation: When they hear slanderous talk, they turn away from it, saying, “We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours
phrases.explanation: When these believers hear vain or abusive talk, they turn away from it. The commentary explains the talk as false speech, additions falsely attributed to Allah's Book, or insults from persecutors. Instead of answering in kind, they say that their deeds belong to them and the others' deeds belong to them. Turning away is not weakness. It is a refusal to let ignorant speech determine their own conduct.

phrases.translation: Peace ˹is our only response˺ to you! We want nothing to do with those who act ignorantly
phrases.explanation: They answer with peace and say they do not seek the ignorant. The commentary explains this as a guarantee that no reviling or hurtful words will come from them, and a refusal to desire dispute with people of ignorance. Their response sets a boundary without aggression. They leave judgment over deeds to Allah and preserve their own dignity by not joining in the folly they hear.

phrases.translation: You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told that he cannot guide everyone he loves or desires to guide. The commentary connects the verse with reports about his uncle Abu Talib, who refused to profess faith at death despite the Prophet's appeal. The statement is therefore both a general principle and a personal consolation. Affection and kinship do not give the Prophet power to create faith in another heart.

phrases.translation: but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills, and He knows best who are ˹fit to be˺ guided
phrases.explanation: Guidance belongs to Allah, who guides whom He wills and knows best who are fit to be guided. The commentary explains this as granting success in faith and steadfastness according to His foreknowledge. The verse does not deny the Prophet's mission, since he conveys the message fully. It distinguishes conveying guidance from producing it in the heart, and leaves the outcome with Allah's wisdom.

phrases.translation: They say ˹to the Prophet˺, “If we were to follow ˹true˺ guidance with you, we would certainly be snatched away from our land
phrases.explanation: The Quraysh say that if they follow the Prophet's guidance, they will be snatched away from their land. The commentary explains their fear as political. If they abandon the idols, they expect other tribes to unite against them, raid them, and drive them out. One report says they even acknowledged his message but feared the consequences. Their objection treats security as more important than truth.

phrases.translation: Have We not established for them a safe haven ˹in Mecca˺ to which fruits of all kinds are brought as a provision from Us
phrases.explanation: Allah reminds them that He established a secure sanctuary in Mecca. The commentary says bloodshed was forbidden there and its people were protected from raids, killing, and captivity, while people around them were not safe. Fruits from every land were gathered there as provision from Allah. The same place they fear losing is already preserved by the Lord they are being asked to worship.

phrases.translation: But most of them do not know ˹this favour˺
phrases.explanation: Most of them do not recognize this favor. The commentary says they do not know that Allah is the One who gave them security and provision, so they remain ungrateful and unbelieving. Their fear of losing the land ignores the power that keeps it safe. The phrase therefore turns their own sanctuary into evidence against them, since the protection they rely on comes from the God they refuse to acknowledge.

phrases.translation: ˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed that had been spoiled by their ˹comfortable˺ living
phrases.explanation: Allah asks the Prophet to consider how many societies were destroyed after their comfortable living made them insolent. The commentary describes such people as intoxicated by abundance, transgressing all bounds, plunging into disobedience, and denying their Lord. Prosperity itself is not condemned, but prosperity that produces heedlessness becomes destructive. Blessing turns into a cause of ruin when it leads people to forget the Giver.

phrases.translation: Those are their residences, never inhabited after them except passingly. And We ˹alone˺ were the Successor
phrases.explanation: Their dwellings remain largely uninhabited after them, and Allah alone is the Successor. The commentary says most of the homes fell into ruin, with only a small part still occupied, and that no human heir truly inherited what was destroyed. Ownership returned to Allah, who inherits the heavens and the earth. The abandoned houses stand as evidence that human settlement is temporary.

phrases.translation: Your Lord would never destroy a society until He had sent to its capital a messenger, reciting Our revelations to them
phrases.explanation: Allah would not destroy a town until He sent a messenger to its mother-city, reciting His signs. The commentary identifies the mother-city as Mecca and the messenger as Muhammad, sent to recite the Quran's signs. The principle is that judgment does not come without warning. Revelation establishes the proof first, so people cannot claim that destruction reached them without guidance.

phrases.translation: Nor would We ever destroy a society unless its people persisted in wrongdoing
phrases.explanation: Allah does not destroy a town unless its people are wrongdoers. The commentary says He would not destroy a believing community, but sends punishment because of disbelief and self-wronging. The verse therefore answers the fear expressed earlier. The sanctuary's people are not punished merely for living there, but only if they reject the warning and persist in wrong.

phrases.translation: Whatever ˹pleasure˺ you have been given is no more than ˹a fleeting˺ enjoyment and adornment of this worldly life
phrases.explanation: Whatever people have been given is only the enjoyment and adornment of worldly life. The commentary mentions possessions and children, saying they provide temporary pleasure and display but avail nothing with Allah at the return. The phrase does not deny that these gifts are pleasant. It denies that they last or that they can serve as a final foundation for human hope.

phrases.translation: But what is with Allah is far better and more lasting. Will you not then understand
phrases.explanation: What is with Allah is better and more lasting. The commentary explains this as the reward kept for those who obey Him, better in quality and everlasting in duration. The closing question calls people to use their reason by choosing the enduring abode over the perishable one. The issue is not whether one can enjoy the world, but whether short-lived enjoyment should be preferred to lasting good.

phrases.translation: Can those to whom We have made a fine promise—which they will see fulfilled—be like those who We have allowed to enjoy the pleasures of this worldly life
phrases.explanation: The verse contrasts a person given a good promise with one given only worldly enjoyment. The commentary says the first is the believer, promised the Garden because of obedience, who believes the promise and will certainly receive it. Reports connect the verse to specific early Muslims and opponents, but the principle is wider. A guaranteed future with Allah cannot be compared with temporary pleasure.

phrases.translation: but on the Day of Judgment will be brought ˹for punishment˺
phrases.explanation: The second person enjoys this world but will be brought forward on the Day of Resurrection. The commentary says he forgets the work whose reward Allah promised to the obedient, prefers perishable enjoyment, and then sees the punishment. Being brought forward means being present before Allah's chastisement. The rhetorical question therefore exposes the folly of treating present comfort as though it were the whole story.

phrases.translation: ˹Watch for˺ the Day He will call to them
phrases.explanation: Allah will call out to the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection. The commentary says this is the day when the Lord of majesty addresses those who associated idols and rivals with Him in worldly life. The call is not to inform Him of something hidden but to confront them publicly. What they treated as worship in private or public becomes the subject of judgment.

phrases.translation: Where are those you claimed were My associate-gods
phrases.explanation: Allah will ask where the partners are whom they used to claim. The commentary explains these as the beings they alleged were His associates. The question exposes the emptiness of their claim, since the supposed partners cannot be produced as help or deity. It also reveals the difference between a slogan repeated in life and a reality that can stand before Allah.

phrases.translation: Those ˹misleaders˺ against whom the decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will cry, “Our Lord
phrases.explanation: Those against whom the decree of wrath is justified will cry out to their Lord. The commentary identifies them as the devils who led human beings astray, or more broadly the misleaders who now face the curse they earned. Their cry begins with recognition of Allah's authority, but it comes too late to change their condition. They are forced to answer the question about the partners people followed.

phrases.translation: These ˹followers˺ are the ones we caused to deviate. We led them into deviance, for we ourselves were deviant
phrases.explanation: The misleaders admit that they caused their followers to deviate, just as they themselves were deviant. The commentary says they do not claim innocence or superior guidance. Their confession acknowledges that the error was shared and propagated. This does not remove their responsibility, since leading others astray compounds their own deviation. The question about supposed partners now turns back on those who encouraged false worship.

phrases.translation: We disassociate ourselves ˹from them˺ before You. It was not us that they used to worship
phrases.explanation: They declare themselves free of their followers before Allah and say those people did not worship them. The commentary explains this as a denial of guardianship and support, not a denial that misguidance occurred. The followers had served desires or false objects rather than truly worshipping these leaders. The verse preserves the complexity of misguidance while still holding the deceivers accountable.

phrases.translation: It will be said ˹to the disbelievers˺, “Call upon your associate-gods ˹for help˺
phrases.explanation: The disbelievers will be told to call upon their associate-gods for help. The commentary says these are the gods and rivals they used to invoke besides Allah. The command is a test that exposes their helplessness. What was treated as divine in life is summoned at the moment of greatest need, when no illusion of power can remain.

phrases.translation: So they will call them, but will receive no response. And they will face the punishment, wishing they had been ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.explanation: They will call, but no answer will come. They will then see the punishment and wish they had been rightly guided. The commentary says the sight of chastisement produces regret for not following truth in the world, but the wish is too late. The verse shows the collapse of false worship, since the partners neither respond nor protect, and guidance refused earlier cannot be recovered.

phrases.translation: And ˹watch for˺ the Day He will call to them, asking
phrases.explanation: Allah will call to them again on that Day. The commentary presents this as another public questioning before the polytheists. The repetition of the call intensifies the accountability, moving from the failure of false gods to the response given to Allah's messengers. It reminds the reader that judgment examines both worship and obedience to the message that was sent.

phrases.translation: What response did you give to the messengers
phrases.explanation: Allah will ask what answer they gave to the messengers. The commentary says the messengers called them to affirm Allah's oneness and to free themselves from idols. The question therefore concerns the central demand of revelation. Their response to that demand, not their inherited status or claimed partners, becomes the decisive matter when they stand before Allah.

phrases.translation: They will be too dumbstruck on that Day to ask one another ˹for answers˺
phrases.explanation: On that Day they will be too dumbstruck to question one another. The commentary says the proofs and news will be obscured from them, leaving them without any argument or report by which to escape. They will not even ask about lineage or appeal to kinship as they did in the world. Allah had already given them repeated proof, so silence replaces both excuse and mutual support.

phrases.translation: As for those who repent, believe, and do good ˹in this world˺
phrases.explanation: The exception is for those who repent, believe, and do good deeds. The commentary explains repentance as turning from idolatry and devoting worship to Allah alone, belief as affirming the Prophet, and good deeds as obeying what Allah commanded in the Book and through His messenger. These three elements join a changed allegiance, a true confession, and a life of obedience.

phrases.translation: it is right to hope that they will be among the successful
phrases.explanation: It is right to hope that such people will be among the successful. The commentary says that when Allah uses perhaps, it is here a definite assurance. The successful are those who attain what they desire with Allah and abide in His gardens. The verse therefore offers a real alternative to the silence of the deniers, grounding hope in repentance, faith, and righteous action.

phrases.translation: Your Lord creates and chooses whatever He wills—the choice is not theirs
phrases.explanation: Allah creates whatever He wills and chooses whom He wills. The commentary explains this as His selecting people for guidance, faith, and good deeds according to His knowledge, just as the polytheists selected the best of their possessions for their idols. It rejects the idea that creatures possess an independent choice that overrides His wise election. The verse therefore joins creation, guidance, and authority in Allah's hands.

phrases.translation: Glorified and Exalted is Allah above what they associate ˹with Him˺
phrases.explanation: Allah is glorified and exalted above the partners people ascribe to Him. The commentary says this declares Him free from their shirk and from the lies they invented about Him. The statement follows naturally from the claim that He alone creates and chooses. If creatures cannot rival Him in creation or election, they cannot rightly be treated as His equals in worship.

phrases.translation: And your Lord knows what their hearts conceal and what they reveal
phrases.explanation: Allah knows what people hide in their hearts and what they make public with their words and limbs. The commentary connects this knowledge to His choosing, since He knows both the inward state and outward conduct of His servants. He enables those fit for good and leaves those given to evil to their chosen path. Divine election is therefore not arbitrary but grounded in complete knowledge.

phrases.translation: He is Allah. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him
phrases.explanation: Allah alone is God, and no other object of worship is permissible beside Him. The commentary describes Him as the One to whom all worship is due. The phrase is a direct confession of monotheism after the discussion of guidance and judgment. It gathers the chapter's arguments from creation, revelation, and resurrection into a single declaration about who may be worshipped.

phrases.translation: All praise belongs to Him in this life and the next. All authority is His. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned
phrases.explanation: Praise belongs to Allah in this life and the next, judgment belongs to Him, and all will return to Him. The commentary explains judgment as His adjudication among creatures after death, when He will judge in truth. Praise therefore spans both worlds, not merely moments of blessing. The return to Him gives moral weight to life, since every deed will come before the One who owns all authority.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Imagine if Allah were to make the night perpetual for you until the Day of Judgment
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to ask what would happen if Allah made night continuous until the Day of Resurrection. The commentary says the word for perpetual means unbroken and unceasing, like an endless state of prosperity or affliction. The question removes the ordinary sunrise people take for granted. Without Allah's gift of day, human life would be trapped in darkness.

phrases.translation: which god other than Allah could bring you sunlight? Will you not then listen
phrases.explanation: No god besides Allah could bring sunlight if the night were made permanent. The commentary says the question is meant to be heard and reflected upon, so people recognize that their Lord brings night and day and can remove either when He wills. The appeal to hearing is an appeal to understanding. The regular dawn is evidence that the idols have no power over the order of the world.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹them also˺, “Imagine if Allah were to make the day perpetual for you until the Day of Judgment
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is also told to ask what would happen if Allah made the day continuous until the Day of Resurrection. The commentary explains this as a day with no night to accompany it. The second question mirrors the first, showing that either half of the cycle would become unbearable if it never ended. Human life depends not on light alone but on alternation.

phrases.translation: which god other than Allah could bring you night to rest in? Will you not then see
phrases.explanation: No god besides Allah could bring a night in which people could rest. The commentary points to the visible alternation of night and day as both mercy and proof. People can see that only the One who distinguishes the two has the power to give each its place. Since the favor comes from Him alone, worship and gratitude should not be shared with powerless objects.

phrases.translation: It is out of His mercy that He has made for you the day and night so that you may rest ˹in the latter˺ and seek His bounty ˹in the former˺
phrases.explanation: Allah made night and day out of mercy. The night is dark so bodies can rest from the fatigue of seeking livelihood, while the day is bright so people can move about, see, and seek His provision. The commentary discusses whether the singular pronoun refers to the night specifically or to both together. In either case, the two times serve complementary human needs.

phrases.translation: and perhaps you will be grateful
phrases.explanation: The purpose of this arrangement is that people may be grateful. The commentary says they should thank Allah alone because no partner helped Him provide night, day, rest, and livelihood. Gratitude is therefore not a vague feeling but an acknowledgment that the whole rhythm of life is His gift. The One who receives praise should be the One who gave the favor.

phrases.translation: And ˹watch for˺ the Day He will call to them
phrases.explanation: Allah will call the polytheists again on the Day of Resurrection. The commentary says the Lord will address those who claimed partners for Him in worldly life. The repetition of this question after the signs of night and day gives the warning force. The same people who ignored evident creation will be asked to produce what they asserted.

phrases.translation: Where are those you claimed were My associate-gods
phrases.explanation: The question asks where the partners are whom they used to claim. The commentary explains that these are the beings they alleged were Allah's associates. The inquiry is not a request for information but a judgment on a false claim. Their answer cannot point to any real helper, because the partners existed only in their assertion.

phrases.translation: And We will bring forth a witness from every faith-community and ask ˹the polytheists˺, “Show ˹Us˺ your proof
phrases.explanation: On that Day Allah will bring a witness from every community. The commentary identifies the witness as that community's prophet or messenger, who testifies how his people responded to the message. The deniers are then told to produce their proof for the partners they worshipped. Since the messengers and arguments have already removed every excuse, the demand exposes the emptiness of their case.

phrases.translation: Then they will ˹come to˺ know that the truth is with Allah ˹alone˺
phrases.explanation: They will then know that truth belongs to Allah alone. The commentary says they will recognize that His proof and tidings are true, and they will become certain of lasting punishment.
