The knowledge comes too late to guide them, but it confirms the justice of the judgment. What was disputed in life becomes undeniable in the presence of Allah.

phrases.translation: And whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them
phrases.explanation: The gods and claims they fabricated will fail them. The commentary says the partners they invented in the world will vanish or depart and will not help them. Instead, those falsehoods will harm them and contribute to their punishment. The verse therefore shows the final collapse of idolatry, when the objects of human invention cannot stand beside the truth of Allah.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Korah was from the people of Moses, but he behaved arrogantly towards them
phrases.explanation: Korah belonged to Moses' own people, and the commentary identifies him as a close relative, often a cousin. His nearness to a prophet does not protect him from corruption. The phrase that he behaved arrogantly toward them is explained as overstepping through pride and tyranny, with reports mentioning displays of clothing or the sheer abundance of his wealth. His sin begins in a heart that turns privilege into superiority.

phrases.translation: We had granted him such treasures that even their keys would burden a group of strong men
phrases.explanation: Allah gave Korah treasures so vast that even their keys or storehouses burdened a group of strong men. The commentary records different reports about whether the keys were literal keys or the treasure stores themselves, and about how many men or animals carried them. The point of the image is abundance beyond ordinary capacity. What should have prompted gratitude becomes the occasion for pride.

phrases.translation: ˹Some of˺ his people advised him, “Do not be prideful! Surely Allah does not like the prideful
phrases.explanation: Some of Korah's people warn him not to exult, because Allah does not love those who exult. The commentary explains exultation as arrogant, insolent joy that does not thank Allah for what He has given. The warning is not against happiness itself but against delight that forgets the Giver and despises others. It comes from within his own community, so he cannot claim that no one showed him a better way.

phrases.translation: Rather, seek the ˹reward˺ of the Hereafter by means of what Allah has granted you
phrases.explanation: The people advise Korah to seek the Home of the Hereafter with what Allah has given him. The commentary says wealth should be used in obedience to Allah, so possessions become a means of drawing nearer to Him rather than an end in themselves. This is not a command to despise wealth but to direct it toward its highest purpose. What Allah gives can become provision for the next life.

phrases.translation: without forgetting your share of this world. And be good ˹to others˺ as Allah has been good to you
phrases.explanation: They also tell him not to forget his share of this world and to do good as Allah has done good to him. The commentary preserves several readings of that share, including acting in this life for the Hereafter, seeking lawful provision, or sending surplus ahead while retaining enough. Doing good means spending wealth in its rightful ways. The phrase joins moderate use of the world with generosity shaped by divine generosity.

phrases.translation: Do not seek to spread corruption in the land, for Allah certainly does not like the corruptors
phrases.explanation: The advice ends with a warning not to seek corruption in the land, since Allah does not love corrupters. The commentary explains corruption as transgression against his people and pursuing what Allah has forbidden. Korah's wealth has become socially destructive, not merely personally dangerous. The verse therefore places economic conduct under moral judgment, because arrogance with resources harms the wider community.

phrases.translation: He replied, “I have been granted all this because of some knowledge I have
phrases.explanation: Korah answers that his wealth was given to him because of knowledge he possesses. The commentary explains the claim in different ways, either as expertise he thinks he has or as a belief that Allah favored him because He knew some excellence in him. In either case, the statement turns gift into entitlement. He treats prosperity as proof of his own worth rather than as a test from Allah.

phrases.translation: Did he not know that Allah had already destroyed some from the generations before him who were far superior to him in power and greater in accumulating ˹wealth˺
phrases.explanation: The reply asks whether Korah does not know that Allah destroyed earlier generations stronger than him and greater in accumulated wealth. The commentary argues that if wealth proved Allah's pleasure, those even wealthier people would not have been destroyed. Allah destroys those with whom He is angry, so riches cannot be read as a certificate of divine approval. The argument uses history to correct Korah's false confidence.

phrases.translation: There will be no need for the wicked to be asked about their sins
phrases.explanation: The wicked will not be questioned about their sins. The commentary records several explanations, including that they will be driven into the Fire without a reckoning, that the angels recognize them by their marks, or that they are not asked about the sins of earlier destroyed peoples. The preferred interpretations emphasize their evident guilt. Their fate is clear enough that interrogation would add nothing.

phrases.translation: Then he came out before his people in all his glamour. Those who desired the life of this world wished
phrases.explanation: Korah comes out before his people in full splendor. The commentary preserves many reports about his display, including red, purple, or yellow garments, decorated mounts, and a large entourage. The details vary, but they all depict public luxury meant to be seen. His wealth is no longer hidden in treasuries. It becomes a spectacle that invites admiration and shapes the desires of those watching.

phrases.translation: If only we could have something like what Korah has been given. He is truly a man of great fortune
phrases.explanation: Those who desire the life of this world wish they had what Korah had been given, calling him a man of great fortune. The commentary says they long for the splendor of the world and see in him a tremendous share of it. Their words reveal a scale of value that stops at visible success. They judge his fortune as great without considering his arrogance, his obligation to Allah, or his final end.

phrases.translation: But those gifted with knowledge said, “Shame on you
phrases.explanation: Those given knowledge rebuke the admirers, saying shame on them. The commentary says they call the people to fear Allah and obey Him, correcting the wish for Korah's display. Knowledge here is not mere information but understanding of Allah's reward. It enables them to see through the glitter that has captured the crowd and to challenge the values expressed by the onlookers.

phrases.translation: Allah’s reward is far better for those who believe and do good. But none will attain this except the steadfast
phrases.explanation: They say Allah's reward is better for those who believe and do good, and only the steadfast attain it. The commentary explains that the patient are those who refrain from pursuing worldly splendor, prefer what is with Allah, and strive in obedience. It even says only such people can truly utter this word. The verse contrasts a fortune that can be displayed with a reward that requires endurance.

phrases.translation: Then We caused the earth to swallow him up, along with his home
phrases.explanation: Allah causes the earth to swallow Korah and his home. The commentary includes reports that Moses was given power over the earth after Korah plotted to disgrace him, and that the ground seized Korah and his companions gradually before closing over them. Other reports describe an ongoing descent into the earth. The details differ, but the outcome is clear. The very ground beneath his wealth becomes the instrument of his ruin.

phrases.translation: There was no one to help him against Allah, nor could he even help himself
phrases.explanation: No group can help Korah against Allah, and he cannot even help himself. The commentary explains that he has no army or supporters to turn back the divine punishment, and that those around him abandon him. His wealth, status, and entourage cannot defend him when Allah acts. The phrase reverses the display of strength in the previous verses, since the man surrounded by admirers is left completely helpless.

phrases.translation: And those who had craved his position the previous day began to say, “Ah
phrases.explanation: Those who had wished for Korah's position the day before now cry out in recognition. The commentary explains the difficult opening expression as meaning do you not see or do you not know. Their cry is a change of mind forced by the punishment they have witnessed. What looked like enviable fortune a day earlier is now understood as a danger from which Allah has spared them.

phrases.translation: It is certainly Allah Who gives abundant or limited provisions to whoever He wills of His servants. Had it not been for the grace of Allah
phrases.explanation: They confess that Allah expands or restricts provision for whom He wills, not as proof of a person's worth or dishonor with Him. The commentary says wealth is not given because someone is noble in Allah's sight, nor withheld because someone is lowly. The onlookers therefore correct Korah's earlier claim. Provision is a divine distribution, not a certificate of spiritual merit.

phrases.translation: He could have surely caused the earth to swallow us up! Oh, indeed! The disbelievers will never succeed
phrases.explanation: They add that had Allah not been gracious to them, He could have caused the earth to swallow them too, and they declare that disbelievers do not succeed. The commentary notes accepted readings of the verb, with Allah as the actor in one, and explains success as attaining what they request. Their words turn fear into insight. They recognize both their own escape and the failure of unbelief.

phrases.translation: That ˹eternal˺ Home in the Hereafter We reserve ˹only˺ for those who seek neither tyranny nor corruption on the earth
phrases.explanation: Allah reserves the Home of the Hereafter for those who do not seek exaltation or corruption on earth. The commentary explains exaltation as arrogance against truth, tyranny, or wrongful domination, and corruption as taking property without right or committing disobedience. The condition is therefore about desire as well as action. The final home belongs to people who refuse both pride and harm.

phrases.translation: The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous
phrases.explanation: The ultimate outcome belongs to the righteous. The commentary says this means the Garden is for those who fear Allah, avoid acts of disobedience, and fulfill His obligations. The phrase contrasts the end of Korah with the end prepared for the God-fearing. One gained a spectacular display in the world, while the other receives a lasting home with Allah.

phrases.translation: Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded with what is better
phrases.explanation: Whoever comes with a good deed will receive something better. The commentary identifies the good deed especially with sincere devotion to Allah's oneness and says the better reward is the Garden and everlasting bliss. Some interpreters clarify that nothing is better than sincere faith itself, so the phrase means the good received through it. The reward is therefore a gift beyond what the servant could earn alone.

phrases.translation: And whoever comes with an evil deed, then the evildoers will only be rewarded for what they used to do
phrases.explanation: Those who come with evil deeds will be repaid only for what they used to do. The commentary identifies the central evil deed as associating partners with Allah, while the final clause emphasizes exact requital. Their punishment is not arbitrary or greater than their deeds deserve. The verse sets Allah's generous reward for faith beside strict justice for persistent wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: Most certainly, the One Who has ordained the Quran for you will ˹ultimately˺ bring you back home ˹to Mecca˺
phrases.explanation: The One who gave the Quran to the Prophet will surely bring him to a place of return. The commentary records several interpretations, including Paradise, the Day of Resurrection, death, or Mecca, and prefers a return to his customary place or birthplace, with Mecca in view. The promise consoles the Prophet after opposition. The One who entrusted revelation to him controls his final destination.

phrases.translation: Say, “My Lord knows best who has come with ˹true˺ guidance and who is clearly astray
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to say that his Lord knows best who has come with guidance and who is in clear error. The commentary says the error is manifest to anyone who reflects carefully. The statement does not curse the opponents but places the judgment with Allah. It echoes Moses' earlier reply to Pharaoh, joining the end of the chapter to the pattern of prophetic trust.

phrases.translation: You never expected this Book to be revealed to you, but ˹it came˺ only ˹as˺ a mercy from your Lord
phrases.explanation: The Prophet did not expect the Book to be revealed to him. The commentary says he had no hope of receiving knowledge about past communities or future events so that he could recite it to his people. Its coming is therefore pure mercy from his Lord, not the result of personal ambition. The verse grounds his prophethood in divine kindness rather than human preparation.

phrases.translation: So never side with the disbelievers ˹in their disbelief˺
phrases.explanation: Because the Book is a mercy, the Prophet is told never to support the disbelievers in their unbelief. The commentary explains this as praising Allah for the gift and refusing to become a helper to those who deny Him. The command protects the message from compromise. A revelation given by mercy must not be repaid by alliance with the rejection of its Giver.

phrases.translation: Do not let them turn you away from the revelations of Allah after they have been sent down to you
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is warned not to let the polytheists turn him away from Allah's signs after they have been revealed. The commentary connects this to their demand for a Book like Moses' and says the warning concerns conveying Allah's proofs. Their objections must not distract him from the revelation he has received. The danger is not open persecution alone but being diverted from the message by persistent argument.

phrases.translation: Rather, invite ˹all˺ to ˹the Way of˺ your Lord, and never be one of the polytheists
phrases.explanation: He is instead to call people to his Lord and never be among the polytheists. The commentary explains that abandoning the call and failing to convey the message would be disobedience resembling the deeds of the polytheists. The command is therefore both positive and protective. He must continue inviting to Allah and keep his own worship free from any association of partners.

phrases.translation: And do not invoke any other god with Allah. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told not to invoke any other god with Allah, since no god is worthy of worship but Him. The commentary says no other being may be worshipped alongside the One to whom all worship belongs. The command gathers the chapter's long argument against idols, false partners, wealth, and tyrannical claims into a final instruction about exclusive worship.

phrases.translation: Everything is bound to perish except He Himself. All authority belongs to Him. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned
phrases.explanation: Everything perishes except Allah, all judgment belongs to Him, and all will return to Him. The commentary records interpretations of except His Face as except Himself or except what is done seeking His Face. It says Allah alone judges creation after death, rewarding believers and giving disbelievers what He promised. The chapter ends by placing every perishable claim under the authority of the One who remains.
